chapters.title: Chapter 8 (Part 1) — Prototype Protection: Organizational Requirements
intro: The Prototype Protection module protects **physical prototypes classified as requiring protection**, including vehicles, components and parts. According to the ISA, the owner of the intellectual property for a prototype is considered the owner of the prototype, and the **owner's commissioning department** is responsible for classifying its protection need.

Prototypes classified as requiring **high** or **very high** protection must meet the minimum requirements of this module. In other words, a supplier cannot decide on its own that "this part is not important". The client's classification applies, and it should be confirmed with the client for each order.

ISA 2027 restructured the prototype protection module significantly: 8.1 is now "Organizational requirements", 8.2 is now "Physical and environmental security", sections 8.3–8.5 of ISA 6 were deleted, and new controls such as 8.1.1, 8.1.2, 8.1.4, 8.1.11, 8.1.12 and 8.1.13 were added. Topics such as test vehicles, events and film or photo shoots are now mainly covered by the "order-specific requirements" in 8.1.2.

This chapter covers the 13 controls of 8.1 Organizational requirements. They apply to every company that manufactures or receives vehicles, components or parts that require protection. The next chapter covers 8.2 Physical and environmental security.

items: Prototypes include vehicles, components and parts, for example pre-series vehicles, body panels, lamps, interior parts and electronic modules that are newly developed and not yet publicly launched.
The owner of a prototype is the owner of its intellectual property, usually the vehicle manufacturer (OEM) or the Tier 1 that commissioned the development.
The owner's commissioning department classifies the protection need; prototypes classified as high or very high must meet the minimum requirements of this module.
This module has no separate columns for high / very high requirements. Its controls contain only Must and Should requirements.

controls.title: Prototype protection regulations and responsibilities
controls.q_en: To what extent are regulations for prototype protection defined within the organization and responsibilities established?
controls.q_zh: To what extent are regulations for prototype protection defined within the organization and responsibilities established?
controls.objective: Successful prototype protection requires regulations for implementation and clear responsibilities within the organization.

must: The organization has a released policy clearly defining the goals and specifications of prototype protection.
Periodic review and, if required, revision of the policy is established.
Responsibilities for prototype protection in the organization are defined, documented, and assigned.
The responsible employees are defined and qualified for their task.
The necessary resources are available.
The contact persons are known within the organization and relevant business partners.

controls.refs: No reference standards are listed in the original (in practice, use it together with the ENX TISAX Participant Handbook and the client's prototype protection specifications)
controls.change2027: New control in ISA 2027. ISA 2027.1 also removed the Should requirement of this control; only the Must requirements remain.
explain: 8.1.1 is the "foundation" of the whole prototype protection module. It plays the same role as policy 1.1.1 plus responsibilities 1.2.2 in the Information Security module. The ISA requires a **released** prototype protection policy that clearly states goals and specifications, is reviewed periodically and is revised when needed. Drafts, verbal agreements or clauses that only exist in customer contracts do not count. It must be a document that your own organization has approved and published.

Responsibilities have four layers: responsibilities are defined, documented and assigned; the responsible people are named and qualified; the necessary resources are available; and the contact persons are known both inside the company and to relevant business partners. In practice, many companies give prototype protection to general affairs or quality as a side job, without authority, budget or training. During the assessment, they are then easily questioned on the points "qualified" and "resources".

Note that ISA 2027.1 removed the Should requirement from this control, so the auditor will focus on whether all of the Must requirements above are implemented. The policy can be a separate document or a sub-policy within the ISMS policy framework. Either way, it must cover the goals of prototype protection and the direction for the other controls in 8.1 and 8.2, such as classification, access control, photography, transport, incident reporting and disposal.

"Contact persons are known" is often overlooked. The customer's prototype protection contact, your internal prototype protection manager and the security company's contact person should all be on a contact list. Front-line staff in production, warehousing, logistics and security should know whom to call when something happens. This is also directly linked to the reporting channels in 8.1.11 incident management.
practice: Write a Prototype Protection Policy that covers at least: scope (which sites and projects), protection goals, classification and the principles for related measures, responsibilities of each role, and handling of violations. Have it signed and released by top management.

Appoint a Prototype Protection Officer by a letter of appointment or in the organization chart, and use a RACI chart to show the split of tasks with the CISO, facilities, quality, project managers and security guards.

Define qualification requirements and keep training records for the officer, for example attendance at the customer's prototype protection briefings, TISAX/ISA courses or internal auditor training. Keep certificates or attendance lists.
Plan an annual budget for access control, video surveillance, covering materials, security service contracts, training, etc., and review in the management review whether resources are sufficient.

Create a prototype protection contact list (internal officer, each customer's contact, security control center, site emergency contacts). Post it at security area entrances and in the guard room, and share it with relevant business partners.
Review the policy at least once a year, or after customer requirement changes, organizational changes or incidents. Keep revision and approval records.

questions: Where is your prototype protection policy? Who approved it? When was it last reviewed?
Which protection goals and specifications does the policy define? Does it cover physical, organizational, photography and transport aspects?
Who is responsible for prototype protection? Were they formally appointed? What qualifications or training do they have?
How are resources for prototype protection (people, budget, equipment) planned and confirmed as sufficient?
Do production staff know who the prototype protection contact is? Do your customers know who your contact is?
When the policy is revised, how are relevant staff and business partners informed?
evidence: Approved and released Prototype Protection Policy with revision history.
Letter of appointment, organization chart or RACI chart for the prototype protection officer.
Training records and proof of qualification of the officer.
Management review minutes that discuss prototype protection resources.
Prototype protection contact list and records of its posting or distribution.
findings: The policy is only a draft or a copy of the customer's specification and was never approved and released by the organization's management.
The policy has not been reviewed for years and still refers to departments that no longer exist or to old ISA numbers.
Prototype protection is handled by general affairs as a side job, without formal assignment or any related training records.
Front-line guards and warehouse staff do not know whom to report to when a prototype incident happens.

controls.tip: I always tell clients that the prototype protection officer is not just a name on paper. The auditor will talk to this person directly. If they cannot explain the key points of the policy or do not know how many customer projects are on site, this control is already in danger.

controls.title: Order-specific requirements for handling prototypes
controls.q_en: To what extent are order-specific requirements and specifications for handling prototypes regulated?
controls.q_zh: To what extent are order-specific requirements and specifications for handling prototypes regulated?
controls.objective: It is important that there is a common understanding of the division of responsibilities and that the implementation of all security requirements is ensured. Due to different client-specific requirements when dealing with prototypes, detailed coordination between the client and contractor is necessary in addition to the overarching implementation of measures to protect prototypes.

must: For each relevant order and associated prototypes, order-specific requirements are agreed with the customer and known to the relevant acting employees. The following aspects are considered: – Security classification and associated security measures of the respective order; – Specifications for camouflage, including specifications for changes to camouflage; – Specifications and security concepts for the use of prototypes on test sites; – Specifications for handling prototypes on public roads; – Specifications and security concepts for events with prototypes; – Specifications and security concepts for film/photo shoots with prototypes; – Specifications for the transport of the prototypes (incl. logistics specifications); – Requirements for the use of subcontractors; – Specifications for handling prototype-relevant information on portable storage media.

controls.refs: No reference standards are listed in the original (in practice, use it together with the ENX TISAX Participant Handbook and the client's prototype protection specifications)
controls.change2027: New control in ISA 2027. Sections 8.3–8.5 of ISA 6 (test vehicles, events, film and photo shoots, etc.) were deleted; these topics are now covered by the "order-specific requirements" in this control.
explain: 8.1.2 is one of the most important changes in the ISA 2027 prototype module. ISA 6 had separate sections such as 8.3 test vehicles and 8.4 events and shoots. ISA 2027 deleted them and instead requires you to agree specific requirements with the customer **for each relevant order**. So test sites, public road testing, events, shoots and transport have not disappeared. They have become topics you must "clarify with the customer per order and make known to the people doing the work".

The ISA lists nine aspects to consider: security classification and related measures, camouflage and changes to camouflage, test sites, public roads, events, film and photo shoots, transport and logistics, subcontractors, and portable storage media. Not every order involves all nine. For example, a Tier 2 that only makes interior parts will not do road tests. But you must be able to show that you considered each aspect and decided "not applicable for this order", rather than never thinking about it.

"Known to the relevant acting employees" is an easy point to fail. If the sales or project manager keeps the customer's confidentiality annex in their mailbox, while the line leader and the truck driver do not know that the part must be covered with black cloth and shipped in a closed truck, the requirement is not met. Order requirements must be turned into work instructions that people on the shop floor can understand.

The camouflage specifications explicitly mention "changes to camouflage". If the camouflage wrap of a test vehicle or the cover of a part is damaged or needs a different design, it must be handled according to the customer's rules. You cannot just patch it with tape and drive on. This links to "damage to camouflage" in 8.1.11 incident management.
practice: Create a "prototype order requirements checklist" that covers the nine aspects one by one: applicable / not applicable, customer requirement, internal measure, owner. Make it a mandatory document when opening each prototype order.
Add a classification field (for example high / very high) to prototype orders in the ERP or project management system so that purchasing, production planning, warehousing and shipping can all see it.

Turn customer requirements into shop-floor work instructions, for example: "Project A parts must be shipped in opaque packaging, with seal numbers recorded, by the designated carrier in a closed truck."

Portable storage media rules: prototype-related files may only be stored on encrypted USB drives or company-approved encrypted devices. Private USB sticks are forbidden. Align this with the media handling controls of the Information Security module.
If test sites, road tests, events or shoots are needed, write a project-level execution plan based on the customer's security concept and confirm it with the customer contact before starting.
Explain the order-specific requirements to all participants at the project kick-off meeting, and keep the attendance list and briefing records.

questions: Please pick a prototype order currently on site and explain which specific requirements you agreed with the customer.
What is the classification of this order? Which security measures did you take for it?
If camouflage or a cover is damaged, which rules do you follow? Who can decide on a replacement?
Who is responsible for transporting prototypes? Does the logistics provider know the requirements?
How do shop-floor workers learn about the special requirements of this order?
May prototype-related data be stored on USB drives? What are the rules?
evidence: Prototype order requirements checklist, or the customer's confidentiality annex or security requirements specification.
Screenshot of the order classification field in the ERP or project system.
Shop-floor work instructions, packaging and transport rules.
Attendance list and slides of the project kick-off meeting.
Security concepts and execution plans for test sites, events or shoots (if applicable).
findings: Customer requirements exist only in the sales mailbox and were never turned into shop-floor rules; production staff do not know the special requirements.
There is no distinction between orders; all prototypes follow the same generic approach, and there is no proof that requirements were agreed with the customer case by case.
Prototypes are shipped with a normal freight service, and the transport requirements were never evaluated.
Engineers carry prototype drawings and photos on private USB sticks.

controls.tip: In my experience, a one-page order checklist is the most useful tool. Tick the nine aspects one by one and write a reason when something does not apply. When the auditor finds this sheet, they usually smile.

controls.title: Training and awareness for handling prototypes
controls.q_en: To what extent do employees and project members evidently participate in training and awareness measures regarding the handling of prototypes?
controls.q_zh: To what extent do employees and project members evidently participate in training and awareness measures regarding the handling of prototypes?
controls.objective: In trainings/awareness seminars on the subject of prototype protection, employees must obtain the necessary knowledge and skills for a security-conscious handling of vehicles, components and parts classified as requiring protection.

must: Regular (at least annual) training of employees regarding the handling of prototypes.
Training of employees and project participants in the handling of prototypes at the start of projects.
Mandatory participation of all employees involved in the project in the training and awareness-raising measures.
The completed measures are to be documented.
The training concept for prototype protection is an integral part of the general training concept (see also control question 2.1.3 Information security).

controls.refs: No reference standards are listed in the original (in practice, use it together with the ENX TISAX Participant Handbook and the client's prototype protection specifications)
controls.change2027: ISA 2027 completely reorganized the prototype protection chapter: the organizational requirements are now 8.1, and the organizational controls of the former ISA 6 section 8.2 were merged in and renumbered. This control corresponds to the training control of the former organizational requirements section; its content is largely unchanged.
explain: The key word in this control is "evidently", meaning participation must be **provable**. Saying "we do training" is not enough. The auditor wants to see records of both annual training and project-start training, and proof that everyone involved in the project took part.

The ISA names two points in time: regular training at least once a year, and training at the start of a project. The first covers general rules, such as the photography ban, access rules and visitor escorting. The second covers order-specific requirements, meaning what you agreed with the customer under 8.1.2. You need both.

"Mandatory participation" means attendance is compulsory, so you need make-up sessions for people who were absent and for new hires. The ISA also requires prototype training to be part of the general training concept and refers to Information Security control 2.1.3. Do not build a separate system. Instead, include a prototype protection module in the company's annual training plan and manage attendance and effectiveness with the same mechanism.

"Project participants" are not only employees. They can also be temporary agency workers, resident engineers, outsourced cleaners or security guards. Anyone who comes into contact with prototypes should be included in the training scope.
practice: Include a "Prototype protection" course in the annual training plan, at least once a year, covering the policy, classification, access control, photography ban, visitor escorting, incident reporting and disposal.
Hold an order-specific briefing at project start to explain the customer's special requirements, and ask participants to sign a statement that they understood them.
Track people and course completion with an LMS or an Excel training matrix. People who have not completed training may not enter prototype security areas; this can be linked to access authorization.
Design a short quiz or scenario questions, such as "A visitor wants to take photos in the showroom. What do you do?", as evidence of training effectiveness.
Provide a short version of the training for agency workers, resident contractors and security guards, and keep attendance records.
Use morning meetings, posters, door signs and digital displays for ongoing awareness reminders.

questions: Please show this year's attendance records and training material for prototype protection training.
When a new project starts, how do project members learn about the customer's special requirements? Are there records?
How do people who were on leave and new hires get make-up training?
How do you confirm that everyone involved in the project has completed training?
How is prototype training integrated into the company's overall training plan?
Have security guards or agency workers received prototype-related training?
evidence: Annual training plan (including the prototype protection module).
Training material, attendance lists, e-learning completion reports.
Records of project kick-off briefings and signed statements.
Training matrix or records linked to access authorization.
Quiz results or training effectiveness evaluation.
findings: Only general annual training exists; there are no records of project-specific training at project start.
The training list does not match the people who actually handle prototypes; some project members were not trained.
Agency workers and resident engineers are not included in the training scope.
Prototype training runs on its own and is not part of the company's general training concept.

controls.tip: It is best to compare training records with the access control list. If someone on the access list has never been trained, the auditor will find it with one quick sample.

controls.title: Qualification of employees working in prototype areas
controls.q_en: To what extent is the qualification of employees for working in prototype areas ensured?
controls.q_zh: To what extent is the qualification of employees for working in prototype areas ensured?
controls.objective: Competent, reliable and trustworthy employees are key to protecting prototypes in the organization. Therefore, it is important to check the suitability of potential employees (e.g. applicants) to an appropriate extent.

must: Sensitive work fields and jobs are determined.
The requirements for employees with respect to their job profiles are determined and fulfilled.
The identity of potential employees is verified (e.g. checking identity documents).
should: The personal suitability of potential employees is verified by means of simple methods (e.g. job interview).

controls.refs: No reference standards are listed in the original (in practice, use it together with the ENX TISAX Participant Handbook and the client's prototype protection specifications)
controls.change2027: New control in ISA 2027.
explain: 8.1.4 is a new control in ISA 2027. The idea is close to employee screening (2.1.1) in the Information Security module, but it focuses on prototype areas. The first step is to **identify sensitive work areas and jobs**, such as the prototype assembly line, the pre-series workshop, the prototype warehouse, test drivers, prototype logistics and photographers.

The second step is to define requirements for these jobs and make sure they are met, for example completed prototype training, a signed confidentiality undertaking, specific skills or a driving license. The third step is identity verification. Usually this means checking the national ID card, passport or residence permit at hiring; for agency workers, the agency provides records of the identity checks.

The Should requirement is to check personal suitability by simple methods, such as a job interview. The ISA deliberately says "simple methods". It does not require background checks or police clearance certificates. In practice, respect the limits set by your national data protection and employment laws (for example the EU GDPR, or Taiwan's PDPA): only collect data that is necessary, and get consent.

Many companies forget agency and contractor staff. If they work in prototype areas, the same sensitive-job requirements apply. The agency contract should require the agency to carry out identity checks, and your company should confirm their training and confidentiality status.
practice: Make a list of sensitive prototype-related jobs, such as pre-series assembly, prototype warehouse staff, test drivers, prototype photographers and prototype logistics, and mark them in the job descriptions.
Define qualification requirements for sensitive jobs: completed prototype training, signed confidentiality obligation, required skills or certificates. HR checks these before hiring.
Check identity documents at hiring and keep a record of the check (for example a tick box and the checker's signature; you do not need to keep a copy, which reduces data protection risk).
Add a suitability section to the interview evaluation form, for example integrity, awareness of confidentiality and previous work experience.
Require the staffing agency, by contract, to perform identity checks and to provide updated staff lists.
When people are transferred into sensitive jobs, confirm again that the qualification requirements are met.

questions: How do you define which jobs are sensitive prototype jobs?
What are the qualification requirements for sensitive jobs? Who checks them?
How do you verify the identity of new employees? And of agency workers?
Do you evaluate suitability in job interviews? Are there records?
When someone transfers internally into a prototype area, what is the confirmation procedure?
evidence: List of sensitive jobs and job descriptions.
Hiring checklist (identity check, signed confidentiality obligation, training completed).
Interview evaluation records.
Identity check clauses in agency contracts and the staff lists.
findings: Sensitive jobs were not identified; everyone is treated the same, and the company cannot explain any special requirements for staff in prototype areas.
Identity checks for agency workers are left entirely to the agency; the company has no confirmation records.
Internal transfers into prototype areas are not re-checked for qualification.

controls.tip: The sensitive jobs list does not need to be complicated. One table with job, requirements and how they are checked is enough. What matters is that HR and the prototype protection officer both agree on it.

controls.title: Non-disclosure agreements and obligations
controls.q_en: To what extent are non-disclosure agreements/obligations existent according to the valid contractual law?
controls.q_zh: To what extent are non-disclosure agreements/obligations existent according to the valid contractual law?
controls.objective: When transmitting information classified as requiring protection, it must be ensured that external organizations are obliged to meet the information security requirements and that the related necessary measures are implemented. The necessary legal basis for this obligation is provided by non-disclosure agreements. Hence, it must be ensured that information classified as requiring protection is transmitted only if such a non-disclosure agreement has been entered and is legally effective.

must: Non-disclosure agreements between contractor and customer (company level), and with all employees and project members exist.
Country-specific legal provisions regarding data protection are to be observed.

controls.refs: No reference standards are listed in the original (in practice, use it together with the ENX TISAX Participant Handbook and the client's prototype protection specifications)
controls.change2027: ISA 2027 completely reorganized the prototype protection chapter: the organizational requirements are now 8.1, and the organizational controls of the former ISA 6 section 8.2 were merged in and renumbered. This control corresponds to the non-disclosure agreement control of the former organizational requirements section.
explain: Non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) exist at two levels: the **company level** is the NDA between you and the customer, and the **individual level** is the confidentiality obligation between you and all employees and project members. Both must exist, and both must be legally effective under the applicable local contract law.

The ISA adds that the employees' confidentiality obligation can be written into a clause of the employment contract. In that case, a separate project-level NDA is only needed for people who are not covered by the general clause or who have separate cooperation agreements. This can greatly reduce paperwork.

The ISA also reminds us that every organization must know the value of the information it receives, such as trade secrets, information on critical business processes, know-how and patents. These are called information values. The client must name them, and they must be handled and protected according to their protection needs throughout the whole project life cycle.

"Observe country-specific data protection law" means that personal data collected when signing NDAs, such as ID numbers, signatures and contact details, must also be processed according to your national data protection law (for example the EU GDPR, or Taiwan's PDPA). In addition, many trade secret laws (for example the EU Trade Secrets Directive or Taiwan's Trade Secrets Act) require "reasonable secrecy measures", and NDAs are important evidence of them.
practice: Keep an NDA register that lists the company-level NDA of each customer: signing date, validity period, covered projects, storage location and expiry reminder.
Check whether the confidentiality clauses in employment contracts or work rules cover prototype information and clearly stay valid after employees leave.
Have people who are not covered by an employment contract, such as agency workers, interns, consultants and resident contractors, sign an individual confidentiality undertaking.
At project start, confirm that the customer NDA is in force before drawings, samples or prototypes are handed over; you can add a checkpoint to the ERP project opening process.
Have the legal team review NDA templates for compliance with national contract and trade secret law. For international customers, confirm the governing law and jurisdiction.
Apply data minimization to the personal data collected in confidentiality undertakings, and inform people of the purpose of collection.

questions: Please show the company-level NDA with this prototype customer.
Where is the employees' confidentiality obligation written down? Does it remain valid after they leave?
How do agency workers and interns sign a confidentiality obligation?
Have you ever received prototypes or drawings before the NDA was in force? How is this controlled?
What happens when an NDA expires? Who tracks this?
evidence: Original customer NDA or e-signature record, and the NDA register.
Confidentiality clauses in employment contracts or work rules.
Confidentiality undertakings of agency workers, contractors and interns.
NDA check records in the project opening process.
findings: The NDA has expired and was not renewed, but prototypes are still being received.
Agency workers have not signed any confidentiality document and are not covered by an employment contract.
The confidentiality clause does not cover obligations after leaving the company.
No NDA register can be shown; NDAs must be searched for in various sales mailboxes.

controls.tip: The biggest risk with NDAs is that they expire and nobody notices. I recommend putting them in a contract management system with expiry reminders. That is much more reliable than the memory of the sales team.

controls.title: Requirements for commissioning subcontractors
controls.q_en: To what extent are requirements for commissioning subcontractors known and fulfilled?
controls.q_zh: To what extent are requirements for commissioning subcontractors known and fulfilled?
controls.objective: When involving subcontractors, the minimum requirements for prototype protection must be met.

must: Approval by the original customer.
Contractually valid non-disclosure agreements exist between contractor and subcontractor (company level) and with all employees and project members.
Ensuring compliance with the security requirements of the actual customer (proof is obtained).

controls.refs: No reference standards are listed in the original (in practice, use it together with the ENX TISAX Participant Handbook and the client's prototype protection specifications)
controls.change2027: ISA 2027 completely reorganized the prototype protection chapter: the organizational requirements are now 8.1, and the organizational controls of the former ISA 6 section 8.2 were merged in and renumbered. This control corresponds to the subcontractor control of the former organizational requirements section.
explain: Subcontracting is a high-risk step for prototype leaks. For example, when you send a prototype housing to an external paint shop or send parts to a third-party lab for testing, the prototype leaves your area of protection. 8.1.6 requires three things: approval by the original customer, an effective NDA with the subcontractor, and assurance that the subcontractor meets the original customer's security requirements, with **proof obtained**.

"Approval by the original customer" is important. Your customer may be a Tier 1, while the real owner of the prototype is the OEM. The approval should trace back to the prototype owner or to a party authorized by contract, preferably in writing.

A common way to "obtain proof" is to require the subcontractor to hold a suitable TISAX label (for example a prototype-related label), or to audit the subcontractor yourself and keep the report. In practice, many OEMs require subcontractors to obtain TISAX as well. Follow your customer's requirements.

This control works together with "requirements for the use of subcontractors" in 8.1.2: the order-specific requirements first clarify whether subcontracting is allowed and to whom, and 8.1.6 confirms that the process is actually followed.
practice: Create a "prototype subcontracting request form": scope of work, subcontractor name, prototype classification, customer approval document, NDA status and security proof, approved by the prototype protection officer.
Get written approval from the original customer (email or formal document) before subcontracting, and store it in the project folder.
Sign a company-level NDA with the subcontractor and require the subcontractor to ensure that its employees have confidentiality obligations.
Ask the subcontractor to share its TISAX assessment result (via the ENX portal) or to accept an audit by you, and record the audit results and follow-up of improvements.
Keep a list of approved subcontractors, showing the prototype classification each may handle and the validity of their proof.
Transport and handover for subcontracting follow the transport requirements of 8.1.2; check and sign at each handover.

questions: Which prototype-related work is currently subcontracted? Who are the subcontractors?
Please show the record of the customer's approval for this subcontracting.
Where is your NDA with the subcontractor? Do the subcontractor's employees also have confidentiality obligations?
How do you prove that the subcontractor meets the customer's security requirements?
When does the subcontractor's TISAX label expire? Who tracks this?
evidence: Subcontracting requests and approval records, written customer approval.
NDA with the subcontractor.
The subcontractor's TISAX assessment result or audit report.
List of approved subcontractors.
findings: Prototype processing was subcontracted without approval from the original customer.
The subcontractor only has a general purchase contract with no confidentiality clauses.
No proof at all can be provided that the subcontractor meets the security requirements.
Work continues to be given to a subcontractor whose TISAX label has expired.

controls.tip: The scariest case I have seen: a prototype housing was sent to an external paint shop, and the owner posted photos of the finished part on Facebook to show off. One extra step for approval and proof before subcontracting can save you.

controls.title: Process for granting access to security areas
controls.q_en: To what extent is a process defined for granting access to security areas?
controls.q_zh: To what extent is a process defined for granting access to security areas?
controls.objective: A process is defined for the protection against unauthorized access to security areas where vehicles, components or parts classified as requiring protection are manufactured, processed, or stored.

must: Responsibilities for access authorization are clearly specified and documented.
A process for new assignments, changes and revocations of access rights is in place.
Code of conduct in case of the loss/theft of access control means are defined and known to the employees.
There is a procedure in place for disabling lost/stolen access control mechanisms (i.e. disabling electronic badges, changing physical locks, etc.) as soon as possible.

controls.refs: No reference standards are listed in the original (in practice, use it together with the ENX TISAX Participant Handbook and the client's prototype protection specifications)
controls.change2027: ISA 2027 completely reorganized the prototype protection chapter: the organizational requirements are now 8.1, and the organizational controls of the former ISA 6 section 8.2 were merged in and renumbered. This control corresponds to the access rights process control of the former organizational requirements section.
explain: 8.1.7 covers the "process", while 8.2.5 covers the "technical means". This control asks who may approve access to security areas, how access rights are added, changed and revoked, and what to do when an access card or key is lost.

The life cycle of access rights must be complete: request when joining the company or a project, adjust when the job changes or the project ends, revoke when the person leaves. The most common problem is that rights are not withdrawn after a project ends, so many people can still enter the prototype area.

Loss or theft has two levels. The first is the employees' code of conduct, for example reporting a loss immediately to the guards or the prototype protection officer. The second is the organization's procedure, for example disabling the electronic card or changing the lock cylinder as soon as possible. With physical keys, changing locks is expensive, so key control must be even stricter.

We recommend a regular review of access rights (for example quarterly) that compares the access control system list with the HR list of current employees and the project lists. This is not a Must in the ISA, but it is the best way to prove that the process works.
practice: Write a procedure for access to prototype security areas that defines how rights are requested, who approves them (for example the area owner), who activates them (for example facilities or the guards) and when they are revoked.
Use an access request form or electronic workflow with fields for requester, area, period, reason and approver.
Make the HR leaver and transfer process automatically notify the access administrator to revoke rights; the project manager requests revocation when a project ends.
Define rules for lost access cards or keys and print them in the employee handbook and on the back of the badge: report immediately to the given extension and contact.
When the guard room receives a loss report, the guards disable the card in the access control system immediately and record the time; for lost physical keys, evaluate whether locks must be changed.
Every quarter, compare the access list with the lists of current employees and project members, and keep records of the review.

questions: Who can approve access to prototype security areas? Is this documented?
Please pick an employee who left recently and show when their access rights were revoked.
What happens to the access rights of project members when a project ends?
What should employees do if they lose their access card? Do they know?
Please show the record of the most recent lost card case.
evidence: Access management procedure.
Records of granting, changing and revoking rights.
Records of lost card reports and card deactivation.
Records of periodic access rights reviews.
findings: Access cards of people who left are still valid weeks later.
No reporting procedure for losses is defined; employees do not know whom to contact if they lose their card.
Access rights are activated by the guards on verbal request, without approval records.

controls.tip: Comparing the leavers list with the access control system is the auditor's favorite trick. In five minutes, they can see whether the process really works.

controls.title: Visitor management (registration and escorting)
controls.q_en: To what extent are regulations for visitor management (including registration and escorting of visitors) in place?
controls.q_zh: To what extent are regulations for visitor management (including registration and escorting of visitors) in place?
controls.objective: Protection against unauthorized access to security areas where vehicles, components or parts classified as requiring protection are manufactured, processed, or stored, including traceable documentation.

must: Registration obligation for all visitors.
Documented non-disclosure obligation prior to access.
Publication of security and visitor regulations.
Country-specific legal provisions regarding data protection are to be observed.

controls.refs: No reference standards are listed in the original (in practice, use it together with the ENX TISAX Participant Handbook and the client's prototype protection specifications)
controls.change2027: 8.1.7 of ISA 6 moved to 8.1.8 in ISA 2027. ISA 2027.1 added "including traceable documentation" to the objective.
explain: In ISA 2027, visitor management moved from the physical section to the organizational requirements section and became 8.1.8. ISA 2027.1 then added "including traceable documentation" to the objective. This means registration alone is not enough. You must be able to **trace** who came, when, whom they visited, which areas they entered and when they left.

There are four Must requirements. All visitors must register, with no exceptions, including senior customer managers and group executives. A documented non-disclosure obligation is needed before access, usually a visitor confidentiality undertaking or a confidentiality statement signed on the registration form. Security and visitor rules must be published, for example posted at the main gate and at reception. And registration data must comply with data protection law.

The control title mentions "escorting". It is not listed as a separate Must item, but based on the title and objective, auditors expect visitors to be escorted by an employee at all times when they enter prototype security areas.

On data protection: do not let later visitors see the data of earlier visitors on the registration form, and define a retention period after which the data is destroyed. For electronic visitor systems, pay attention to account permissions and data retention periods.
practice: Introduce a visitor registration system or paper visitor book with fields for name, company, host, areas entered, entry and exit time, ID check and signed confidentiality statement.
Integrate the visitor confidentiality statement into the registration process; no visitor badge is issued without a signature.
Use badge colors to show which areas a visitor may enter. In prototype areas, the host must escort the visitor at all times, and the badge is collected when the visitor leaves.
Post the visitor rules at the main gate and reception: no photography, camera lenses sealed, escort at all times, do not leave the group.
Define a retention period for visitor data (for example one year, according to the company's data protection policy), destroy it when the period ends and keep a record of the destruction.
For paper registration, use one sheet per visitor or a covered design so that later visitors cannot see earlier entries.

questions: Please show the visitor records for the last week.
Where do visitors sign the confidentiality obligation before entering?
Who escorts visitors in prototype areas? How is this recorded?
Where are the visitor rules published?
How long is visitor data kept? How is personal data protected?
Do senior customer managers also have to register when they visit?
evidence: Visitor records (with entry and exit times, host and areas).
Records of signed visitor confidentiality statements.
Photos of posted visitor rules.
Rules and records for retention and destruction of visitor data.
findings: Group executives or well-known customers do not have to register.
The registration form has no confidentiality statement; visitors sign nothing before entering prototype areas.
The paper visitor book lies open, and anyone can see the names and phone numbers of all visitors.
Visitor records only show the entry time, not the exit time, so visits cannot be traced.

controls.tip: When I do consulting, the sentence I hear most is: "He is a friend of the boss, he doesn't need to register." And of course, that is the day the auditor is standing at the main gate. A rule is only a rule if it applies to everyone.

controls.title: Carrying and using mobile recording devices
controls.q_en: To what extent is a regulation for carrying along and using mobile video and photography devices in(to) defined security areas established?
controls.q_zh: To what extent is a regulation for carrying along and using mobile video and photography devices in(to) defined security areas established?
controls.objective: A regulation for the carrying and use of mobile image and sound recording devices in security areas where vehicles, components or parts classified as requiring protection are manufactured, processed or stored is defined. The unauthorized creation or distribution of sound and image material is prevented.

must: Rules for carrying (e.g. with / without sealing, etc.) are in place.
Rules for use (e.g. making phone calls, taking photos, using QR codes, etc.) are in place.

controls.refs: No reference standards are listed in the original (in practice, use it together with the ENX TISAX Participant Handbook and the client's prototype protection specifications)
controls.change2027: ISA 2027 completely reorganized the prototype protection chapter: the organizational requirements are now 8.1, and the organizational controls of the former ISA 6 section 8.2 were merged in and renumbered. This control corresponds to the control on carrying and using mobile devices in the former organizational requirements section.
explain: Smartphones are the number one channel for prototype leaks. 8.1.9 requires two kinds of rules: **rules for carrying** (may devices be brought in, must the camera be sealed) and **rules for use** (may people make calls, take photos, scan QR codes).

The ISA gives "sealing" as an example. In many plants, the most common method is camera stickers: when entering a security area, special tamper-evident stickers are put on the front and rear cameras of the phone, and when leaving, the guard checks that the stickers are intact. If a sticker has been removed, it leaves a VOID mark, so the guard knows that someone may have taken photos.

Rules for use must be practical. Production may need to scan QR codes to report work, or people may need to take phone calls. So the rule can be: "Phone calls are allowed, but photos and videos are forbidden; QR codes may only be scanned with company-issued devices whose cameras are controlled." The key is that rules are clear, workable and checked by someone.
Do not forget other devices: smartwatches, tablets, laptop webcams, dashcams, action cameras and even smart glasses. Define the scope of the rules as "mobile devices that can record images or sound".
practice: Write rules for mobile devices in security areas that cover phones, tablets, laptops, smartwatches, smart glasses, cameras and any other device that can record.
Install lockers at entrances; in very high areas, phones must be stored in the lockers; in high areas, camera lenses are sealed.
Use camera stickers with a tamper-evident VOID pattern and serial numbers. The guards apply and check them at entry and exit and record them.
Define clear usage rules: calls allowed, photos and videos forbidden, video conferencing forbidden, QR codes only scanned with controlled company devices.
On company-issued work tablets, disable the camera or restrict apps through MDM.
Post pictogram signs at entrances, and include the rules in the 8.1.3 training and the 8.1.8 visitor rules.

questions: May employees bring their phones into prototype security areas? Under what conditions?
Who applies the camera stickers? Who checks them when people leave? What happens if a sticker is damaged?
What do you do when production needs to scan QR codes?
Are there rules for smartwatches or laptop cameras?
How are visitors' phones handled?
evidence: Rules for mobile devices.
Records of issuing and checking camera stickers.
Photos of entrance signs and lockers.
Screenshot of the MDM camera restriction policy.
findings: The rules only forbid photos and say nothing about carrying devices; on the shop floor, nobody's phone is sealed.
Camera stickers can easily be removed and put back, have no tamper-evident design, and nobody checks them when people leave.
The rules do not cover smartwatches, tablets and similar devices.

controls.tip: The biggest risk with camera stickers is that they become a formality. I ask the guards to really turn the phone over and look when people leave. If a sticker shows VOID, they record it and report it. Only then does it deter anyone.

controls.title: Image recording and handling of image material
controls.q_en: To what extent are regulations for image recording and handling of created image material existent?
controls.q_zh: To what extent are regulations for image recording and handling of created image material existent?
controls.objective: Regulations for recording images of vehicles, components or parts classified as requiring protection must be defined in order to prevent unauthorized creation or transmission of such image material.

must: In areas where vehicles, components or parts classified as requiring protection are located, there is a general ban on recording images.
Release by the original client for image recordings of vehicles, components or parts classified as in need of protection.
Approval process for image recording.
A clear documentation of the recordings carried out is available (info who, when, what, where, with what).
Determination by the original client for the classification of image material is obtained in the case of image recordings of vehicles, components or parts classified as requiring protection.
Secure storage of image material.
Secure deletion/disposal of image material no longer required.
Secured transmission/shipping of image material to authorized recipients only.

controls.refs: No reference standards are listed in the original (in practice, use it together with the ENX TISAX Participant Handbook and the client's prototype protection specifications)
controls.change2027: ISA 2027 completely reorganized the prototype protection chapter: the organizational requirements are now 8.1, and the organizational controls of the former ISA 6 section 8.2 were merged in and renumbered. This control corresponds to the image recording control of the former organizational requirements section.
explain: 8.1.9 covers "devices"; 8.1.10 covers "taking pictures and the image material". The principle is a **general ban on recording images**. An exception needs all of the following: release by the original client, an internal approval process, a record of the recording, and the client's decision on how the images are classified. The ISA adds that the release can be given directly or by contractual agreement.

The record of a recording must answer five questions: who took it, when, what, where, and with which device. For example, when quality staff need to photograph a defective part to send to the customer, they should use a company-designated camera or controlled device and record the shot.

The life cycle of images after they are taken must also be managed: secure storage (for example an encrypted project folder with access control), secure transmission (for example an encrypted transfer platform specified by the customer, not a chat app such as WhatsApp or LINE or a private mailbox), and secure deletion when no longer needed, including camera memory cards and device photo galleries.

Many companies overlook "image classification". The photos themselves are information that requires protection. The client decides their classification, and they are then handled according to the classification rules of the Information Security module.
practice: State in the Prototype Protection Policy that photography is forbidden in principle and that exceptions require a request.
Create a "prototype image recording request form": purpose, subject, location, time, photographer, device number, basis of the customer release, image classification, approver.
Provide dedicated recording devices (for example numbered cameras or MDM-controlled tablets), normally kept locked by the prototype protection officer and issued against signature.
Store images in encrypted, access-controlled project folders, such as a restricted SharePoint site or an encrypted NAS share. Storing them on personal devices is forbidden.
Send images via the customer's designated platform or by encrypted transfer; email attachments must be encrypted. Chat apps such as WhatsApp or LINE are forbidden.
Delete images at project end or at the customer's request, including the device memory cards, and keep a deletion record.

questions: What is the process when quality staff need to photograph a defective part?
Please show the latest recording record, including who, when, what, where and with which device.
Where is the basis for the customer's release of photography? Who decides the classification of the images?
Where are the photos stored? Who can access them? How are they sent to the customer?
How are photos that are no longer needed deleted? What about the camera memory cards?
evidence: Recording requests and approval records.
Customer release documents or contract clauses.
Recording logs and device issue records.
Access settings of the image storage location, transmission records, deletion records.
findings: Quality staff photograph defective prototypes with personal phones and share the photos in a chat group (e.g. WhatsApp, LINE, Teams).
A request form exists, but the device used and the recording location are not recorded.
The image classification was not decided by the client.
After the project ended, the memory card of the recording device still holds many prototype photos.

controls.tip: Prototype photos in chat groups are the finding I have seen most often in assessments. One dedicated camera plus one request form costs very little and works very well.

controls.title: Prototype incident management
controls.q_en: To what extent are incident management requirements regulated?
controls.q_zh: To what extent are incident management requirements regulated?
controls.objective: Incidents that could interrupt or jeopardize the continuous protection of vehicles, components and parts classified as in need of protection can occur despite the security measures that have been implemented. In this case, competent, swift action is required to minimize the damage caused and implement appropriate measures in a timely manner.

must: For each order and associated prototypes, procedures for dealing with incidents are agreed with the client and known to the relevant employees. The following aspects are considered: – Breach of secrecy; – Burglary; – Theft; – Breakdowns; – Accidents; – Fire; – Irregularities in transport; – Dealing with authorities and law enforcement officers; – Damage to camouflage.
Handling of incidents with prototypes is – where relevant – also regulated beyond the order period.
General and client-specific reporting obligations and reporting channels are known (internal and client).

controls.refs: No reference standards are listed in the original (in practice, use it together with the ENX TISAX Participant Handbook and the client's prototype protection specifications)
controls.change2027: New control in ISA 2027.
explain: 8.1.11 is a new incident management requirement in ISA 2027 that is specific to prototypes. Unlike 1.6 incident management in the Information Security module, it is agreed with the client **order by order**. The ISA lists nine situations: breach of secrecy, burglary, theft, breakdowns, accidents, fire, irregularities in transport, dealing with authorities and law enforcement officers, and damage to camouflage.

"Dealing with authorities and law enforcement officers" is very practical. If a test vehicle has an accident on the road and the police want to take photos as evidence, or customs want to open a box to inspect a prototype, what should the people on site do? Usually the client provides guidance, for example: identify yourself, ask for the inspection to be done under cover, and immediately inform the client contact.

The second Must says that incident handling may still need rules after the order period ends. For example, prototype photos may leak after the project has ended, or parts of a returned prototype may be found still on site. You must still report according to the agreement.

The third Must is about reporting obligations and channels: whom to report to internally, whom to report to at the client, and within what time. Front-line staff must know this. We recommend putting the contact information on a card or posting it in security areas and in transport vehicles.
practice: For each prototype order, create an "incident response card" that lists the steps, reporting contacts and deadlines for the nine situations, confirmed by the client.
Create a prototype incident report form with fields for time, location, prototype number, incident type, actions taken, and who was informed when.
Include prototype incidents in the company's overall incident management procedure (see Information Security 1.6), but keep the client-specific reporting path.
Transport vehicles and test drivers carry the response card, including what to do at police checks, after accidents and when camouflage is damaged.
State in contracts or project closure documents the reporting obligations and contacts that apply after project closure.
Run a tabletop exercise at least once a year, for example "theft from the pre-series warehouse" or "camouflage wrap torn on the road".

questions: Please pick a prototype order and explain the procedure in case of theft or an accident.
Were these procedures agreed with the client? Where is the evidence?
Do staff on site know whom to report to and within what time?
If police or customs want to inspect a prototype, what do staff on site do?
How are reporting obligations handled if an incident happens after the project ends?
What is your most recent prototype incident or exercise record?
evidence: Order-specific incident procedures or response cards, and records of the client's confirmation.
Incident report forms and handling records.
List of reporting contacts and how it is published.
Exercise records.
findings: There is only a generic information security incident procedure; incident handling was not agreed for prototype orders.
Situations such as dealing with law enforcement or damage to camouflage were not considered.
Front-line transport staff do not know the client's reporting contact.

controls.tip: The exercise does not need to be big. Take one scenario, for example a camouflage wrap torn by the wind on the highway, and ask everyone what the next step is. Usually by step three you discover what you have not thought about.

controls.title: Documentation and traceability of prototypes
controls.q_en: To what extent is comprehensive documentation and traceability of vehicles and components requiring special protection ensured throughout the entire processing procedure?
controls.q_zh: To what extent is comprehensive documentation and traceability of vehicles and components requiring special protection ensured throughout the entire processing procedure?
controls.objective: Continuous protection of vehicles, components and parts classified as in need of protection can only be ensured if their location and the department currently responsible for processing them can be traced at all times.

must: There must be a process/concept for the documentation of vehicles, components and parts classified as requiring protection.
All vehicles, components and parts classified as in need of protection must be documented and changes must be traceable.
Documentation needs to be updated regularly.

controls.refs: No reference standards are listed in the original (in practice, use it together with the ENX TISAX Participant Handbook and the client's prototype protection specifications)
controls.change2027: New control in ISA 2027.
explain: 8.1.12 requires that you can always answer two questions: **where is this prototype now**, and **who is responsible for it now**. This is similar to the asset inventory in information security, but for physical prototypes.

The ISA requires three things: a documented process or concept, documentation of all prototypes requiring protection with traceable changes, and regular updates of the documentation. Changes include movements, handovers between departments and status changes (for example in processing, in testing, waiting for return, scrapped).

In practice, you can track prototypes with batch or serial numbers in the ERP, or with a dedicated prototype register. What matters is that handovers are checked and signed, and that the records connect with the disposal and return records of 8.1.13 to form a complete life cycle.

A common verification method of auditors is the "two-way check between records and items": pick an entry from the register and find the item on site, then pick an item on site and find its record. If the two do not match, it is a non-conformity.
practice: Create a "prototype register": number, customer / project, classification, quantity, current location, responsible department or person, status, last update.
Use transfer slips with signatures for goods receipt, internal transfers, sending to subcontractors, shipping or return, and update the register each time.
Put code labels or QR codes on prototypes that do not reveal their content, so that scanning updates the location. Avoid labels that show the project name directly.
Do a monthly or quarterly stocktake with two-way checks between records and items, and record how differences are resolved.
Keep the register in an access-controlled system with change logs so that changes are traceable.
Handle any differences found according to the incident procedure of 8.1.11.

questions: Please show the prototype register and explain how it is updated.
I am picking this item from the register. Please take me to it on site.
For this part here on site, please find its record in the register.
When a prototype moves from the pre-series line to the test lab, how is the handover recorded?
How often do you do stocktakes? How was the last difference handled?
evidence: Prototype traceability procedure or concept.
Prototype register and change records.
Signed transfer and handover slips.
Stocktake records and records of how differences were handled.
findings: The register only records goods receipt, not internal transfers or the currently responsible department.
Records and items do not match; there are prototypes on site that are not in the register.
The register is a shared Excel file that anyone can change, with no change history.

controls.tip: The two-way check between records and items is something I always do in an assessment. Do it yourself regularly, and your heart will not race on assessment day.

controls.title: Disposal, recycling or return of prototypes and relevant tools
controls.q_en: To what extent is it ensured that vehicles, components, parts and relevant tools classified as in need of protection that are no longer needed are disposed of/ recycled/ returned in accordance with the client's specifications?
controls.q_zh: To what extent is it ensured that vehicles, components, parts and relevant tools classified as in need of protection that are no longer needed are disposed of/ recycled/ returned in accordance with the client's specifications?
controls.objective: It is important for every organization that vehicles, components and parts classified as in need of protection are disposed of, recycled or returned after the use phase according to a specified process. This is to prevent them from falling into unauthorized hands or being disposed of as "standard waste".

must: There is a concept for dealing with classified vehicles, components and parts and relevant tools requiring protection after the use phase. The following aspects are considered: – Specifications for disposal, recycling or return are obtained from the respective client; – Instruction of affected employees about the requirements.
should: Proof of compliance with the specifications is available.

controls.refs: No reference standards are listed in the original (in practice, use it together with the ENX TISAX Participant Handbook and the client's prototype protection specifications)
controls.change2027: New control in ISA 2027.
explain: 8.1.13 deals with the last mile of the prototype life cycle. The ISA stresses that prototypes must not be disposed of as "standard waste". Imagine a prototype bumper thrown into the recycling area behind the plant, and the next day the scrap dealer posts a photo of it online. All your access control and covering would have been for nothing.

This control also covers "relevant tools". According to the ISA, relevant tools are tools made and used specifically for producing prototype parts, because they contain sensitive information related to the design or component, for example body press dies. Tool makers and stamping plants should pay special attention.

The Must requires two things: obtaining the disposal, recycling or return specifications from each client, and making them known to the affected employees. The Should is to keep proof of compliance, for example return receipts, destruction certificates, and before-and-after photos of destruction (photography must follow 8.1.10).

Different customers may have different requirements. Some require everything to be returned, some allow destruction on site followed by recycling, and some require a qualified destruction company that issues a destruction certificate. This also links to the order-specific requirements of 8.1.2.
practice: Add a field "handling after use" to the prototype order checklist: return, destruction on site, external destruction, recycling, with the source of the customer specification.
Set up a locked holding area for prototype scrap, separate from the normal scrap area.
At least two people witness destruction and fill in a destruction record (number, quantity, method, witnesses); for external destruction, get a destruction certificate.
Use a receipt for returns and update the status in the 8.1.12 register.
Include dies and fixtures: keep a register of prototype-related tools, and at project end seal, return or destroy them according to customer specifications.
Explain the prototype disposal rules to warehouse staff, waste handling staff and outsourced cleaners.

questions: How are prototypes that are no longer needed handled? Where are the specifications of each customer?
Please show the record of the most recent destruction or return of prototypes.
What happens to prototype-specific dies at the end of a project?
Do the people who handle waste know that prototypes must not go into normal scrap?
How do you confirm that an external destruction company is trustworthy? Do you have destruction certificates?
evidence: Disposal and return procedure and customer specifications.
Destruction records, destruction certificates, return receipts.
Register of prototype-related tools and records of their disposition.
Records of briefings or training for affected staff.
findings: Defective prototypes are mixed with normal scrap and collected by a normal recycling company.
No customer specification for disposal was obtained; the company decides on its own how to handle it.
Prototype-specific dies are not managed after the project ends and are stored in an open warehouse.

controls.tip: Many companies take good care of the production line but forget the scrap area. During assessments, I walk to the recycling yard behind the plant, and I often find surprises.

summary: The owner's commissioning department classifies the protection need of a prototype; prototypes classified as high or very high must meet the minimum requirements of this module.
ISA 2027 restructured the module: 8.1 Organizational requirements (13 controls), 8.2 Physical and environmental security (7 controls); the former 8.3–8.5 were deleted.
8.1.1 requires a released prototype protection policy, clear responsibilities, qualified staff, resources and known contact persons; 2027.1 removed the Should requirement.

8.1.2: for every relevant order, agree order-specific requirements with the customer (classification, camouflage, test sites, public roads, events, shoots, transport, subcontracting, storage media) and make them known to the people doing the work.
8.1.3–8.1.6 cover training (annually plus at project start), qualification for sensitive jobs, NDAs at company and individual level, and subcontractors (customer approval and proof required).

8.1.7–8.1.10 cover the access rights process, visitor registration and confidentiality (2027.1 stresses traceability), carrying and using mobile devices, and the general ban on photography plus life-cycle management of image material.
8.1.11–8.1.13 cover order-specific incident handling, the prototype register and traceability, and disposal, recycling or return (including relevant tools).
For the mapping between prototype labels and controls, always refer to the latest ENX Participant Handbook.

chapters.title: Chapter 8 (Part 2) — Prototype Protection: Physical and Environmental Security
chapters.title_en: Prototype Protection - Physical and Environmental Security
intro: 8.2 Physical and environmental security applies to all companies that manufacture or store vehicles, components or parts requiring protection **on their own properties**, or that are provided with such prototypes for use. If prototypes are only present on someone else's property, you should confirm the security concept of that property's operator.

The 7 controls in this chapter can be understood as an "onion": the outer layer is the perimeter (8.2.2), then the building's outer skin (8.2.3), then view protection (8.2.4), access control (8.2.5) and intrusion monitoring (8.2.6), and the innermost layer is segregation between customers (8.2.7). 8.2.1 Security concept draws the whole onion as one picture.

Remember these key numbers and requirements: accessible parts of the outer skin must resist simple tools for **at least three minutes**; new developments classified high or very high must **never be viewable by unauthorized persons**; intrusion alarms must go to a **qualified security service or control center**, or there must be **24/7 guarding by a qualified service**, with intervention as a rule within twenty minutes; prototypes of different customers must be segregated, otherwise the customer's explicit approval is required.

blocks.text: The onion model of physical protection

head: Layer
Control
Key point
rows: Six aspects plus perimeter, shown on a floor plan
The sum of measures prevents unauthorized access to the property
Resists simple tools for at least three minutes (see RC2)
High / very high new developments cannot be viewed by unauthorized persons
One of three: mechanical locks, electronic access, personal control, documented
Connected to a qualified security service or 24/7 guards, alarm plans
Segregate by customer / project; exceptions need customer approval

blocks.title: Connect organizational and physical requirements
blocks.text: The access control technology in 8.2.5 must work with the access rights process in 8.1.7; visitor management in the 8.2.1 security concept corresponds to 8.1.8; alarm handling in 8.2.6 must connect to 8.1.11 incident management; and customer approval for missing segregation under 8.2.7 can be agreed together with the 8.1.2 order-specific requirements.

In the physical section, the auditor will always walk around the site, and often outside the building too. Before the assessment, walk around once in daylight and once at night, looking at it with an auditor's eyes.

controls.title: Physical and environmental security concept
controls.q_en: To what extent is a security concept available describing minimum requirements regarding the physical and environmental security for prototype protection?
controls.q_zh: To what extent is a security concept available describing minimum requirements regarding the physical and environmental security for prototype protection?
controls.objective: The necessary measures for prototype protection must be applied to and implemented on properties and facilities of suppliers, development partners and service providers. A security concept must be established by the respective operator. Implementation and observation of the physical and environmental security measures defined in the security concept must be ensured by the responsible operator.

must: A security concept is established. The following aspects are considered: – Stability of outer skin; – View and sight protection; – Protection against unauthorized entry and access control; – Intrusion monitoring; – Documented visitor management; – Client segregation.

controls.refs: No reference standards are listed in the original (in practice, use it together with the ENX TISAX Participant Handbook and the client's prototype protection specifications)
controls.change2027: ISA 2027 renumbered section 8.1 Physical and environmental security of ISA 6 as 8.2 (former 8.1.7 visitor management moved to 8.1.8). This control corresponds to the former 8.1.1.
explain: 8.2.1 is the umbrella of the physical section. It requires the operator to establish a **security concept** that clearly describes six aspects: stability of the outer skin, view protection, protection against unauthorized entry and access control, intrusion monitoring, visitor management and client segregation. The Should adds perimeter security.

A security concept is not a nice slide deck. It must match the real site. We recommend building it around a floor plan that shows the borders of security areas, entrances and exits, access control points, video and intrusion detection points, covering measures and the separation between customers, mapped to controls 8.2.2 to 8.2.7.

The objective mentions "properties of suppliers, development partners and service providers", meaning every place where prototypes are present needs a security concept. If prototypes are temporarily stored in a rented warehouse or at a test site, that location must be included, or you must confirm that its operator has its own security concept.
The security concept should also be reviewed regularly, for example when the site is extended, production lines move or new customer projects start, to confirm that it is still valid.
practice: Write a physical security concept for prototypes, using the site floor plan to mark security areas, perimeter, entrances, access control points, intrusion detection, cameras and covering measures.
Use a table to describe, aspect by aspect, the current measures for the six aspects plus perimeter security and the related controls.
Divide the site into security levels, for example general area, controlled area and prototype security area, and describe the access conditions for each.
For each external location (rented warehouse, test site), confirm the security concept and who is responsible.
Review the security concept every year or when the site changes, and keep version records.

questions: Please show your physical security concept for prototypes and walk me through the floor plan.
How is each of the six aspects implemented?
Which perimeter security measures do you have?
If prototypes are stored in a rented warehouse, how does the security concept cover it?
When was the security concept last updated? Why?
evidence: Physical security concept and marked-up floor plan.
Mapping table of the six aspects.
Security concept review records.
Records confirming the security of external locations.
findings: The security concept only describes access control and does not cover view protection, intrusion monitoring or client segregation.
The floor plan is outdated and does not match the actual layout of security areas on site.
An external warehouse where prototypes are stored temporarily is not included in the security concept.

controls.tip: A security concept works best with a floor plan attached. The auditor walks around with the plan, and if the plan matches the site, the next controls go smoothly.

controls.title: Perimeter security
controls.q_en: To what extent is perimeter security existent preventing unauthorized access to protected property objects?
controls.q_zh: To what extent is perimeter security existent preventing unauthorized access to protected property objects?
controls.objective: Unauthorized access to properties where vehicles, components or parts classified as requiring protection are manufactured, processed, or stored shall be prevented.

must: Unauthorized access to properties is not possible.
The sum of the measures must be suitable to prevent unauthorized access to the protected objects of the property.
should: Appropriate measures are in place such as structural measures (e.g. fence systems, walls, floor count,…), technical measures (e.g. detection, alarm system, technical access systems,...), or natural barriers (e.g. vegetation, ...).

controls.refs: No reference standards are listed in the original (in practice, use it together with the ENX TISAX Participant Handbook and the client's prototype protection specifications)
controls.change2027: ISA 2027 renumbered section 8.1 Physical and environmental security of ISA 6 as 8.2 (former 8.1.7 visitor management moved to 8.1.8). This control corresponds to the former 8.1.2.
explain: The perimeter is the outer layer of the onion. The Must in 8.2.2 focuses on the **result**: unauthorized access to the property must not be possible, and the sum of measures must be enough to prevent unauthorized access to the protected objects. The phrase "sum of the measures" means you can combine several measures that complement each other.

The Should gives three types of measures: structural, such as fences, walls and floor count; technical, such as detection, alarms and access systems; and natural barriers, such as vegetation. Plants in industrial parks often have guards at the main gate but gaps in the side wall, or share a wall with the neighboring plant. Then other measures must make up for it.

"Floor count" is interesting: if the prototype area is on a high floor, that alone makes access harder. For companies in office towers or shared office-and-factory buildings, the perimeter may be the building's access control plus floor-level control.

The perimeter and the 8.2.3 outer skin are two different lines of defense. The perimeter keeps people away from the building; the outer skin keeps them out of it. Where the perimeter of a shared site cannot be controlled, the outer skin and inner security areas must be stronger, and this should be explained in the security concept.
practice: Survey the site perimeter: walls, fences, main gate, side gates, goods entrances and borders with neighboring plants, and mark them on the floor plan.
Have guards and vehicle control at the main gate; keep side gates locked and include them in intrusion detection.
Include fence damage in the routine patrol checklist, and repair and record it as soon as it is found.
Where needed, add perimeter infrared detection, cameras or lighting.
For shared buildings or sites, get the access control and security information from the building management, and describe the additional measures in the security concept.

questions: Which measures make up your perimeter?
How are side gates and goods entrances normally controlled?
Are there gaps in the wall? How are patrols done?
