If the perimeter cannot be fully controlled, how do you compensate?
How is the perimeter monitored at night?
evidence: Perimeter floor plan and description of measures.
Guard patrol records.
Perimeter repair records.
Security contract of the building or site (for shared locations).
findings: A side gate is kept open for long periods to make moving goods easier, with nobody watching it.
The damaged fence was not repaired, and the patrol records are blank.
For a shared building, perimeter risks were not evaluated and there are no additional measures.

controls.tip: I often compare a site to an onion, and the perimeter is the outer skin. A hole in the skin is acceptable, but you need to know where the hole is, and the next layer must be strong enough.

controls.title: Outer skin resistant to break-in (3 minutes)
controls.q_en: To what extent is the outer skin of the protected objects/ security areas constructed such as to prevent removal or opening of outer-skin components using standard tools?
controls.q_zh: To what extent is the outer skin of the protected objects/ security areas constructed such as to prevent removal or opening of outer-skin components using standard tools?
controls.objective: Unauthorized access to objects / security areas where vehicles, components or parts classified as requiring protection are manufactured, processed or stored shall be prevented.

must: Unauthorized access to objects / security areas is not possible.
Easily accessible windows, doors, and other components are designed to prevent break-ins using simple tools such as screwdrivers and pliers for a minimum period of three minutes.
should: Solid construction (e.g. masonry, concrete, reinforced concrete, or prestressed concrete). If the outer skin is not solid, risk mitigating measures must be in place and evidence of a risk-based decision to maintain an insubstantial barrier must exist.

controls.refs: DIN EN 1627 / RC2
controls.change2027: ISA 2027 renumbered section 8.1 Physical and environmental security of ISA 6 as 8.2 (former 8.1.7 visitor management moved to 8.1.8). This control corresponds to the former 8.1.3.
explain: The outer skin means the walls, doors, windows and roof of the building or security area. The Must in 8.2.3 contains one concrete number: easily accessible windows, doors and other components must resist break-in with **simple tools such as screwdrivers and pliers** for **at least three minutes**.

The ISA refers to DIN EN 1627 RC2, the European standard for burglar resistance of doors and windows. RC2 roughly corresponds to resisting an attempt with simple tools for three minutes. Outside Europe, products labeled RC2 may be hard to find. In practice, you can use equivalent security doors, reinforced locks, window security grilles and similar measures, and keep the specifications or the manufacturer's confirmation.

"Easily accessible" is the key point: ground-floor windows, loading doors, emergency exits and roof skylights are common weak spots. In many sheet-metal buildings, the wall panels can be removed in a few minutes with a power screwdriver. Here the risk-mitigating measures from the Should are needed, for example a separate prototype room inside the building or additional intrusion detection.

The Should prefers solid construction such as masonry or concrete. For sheet-metal or light partition walls, risk-mitigating measures are required, and there must be evidence of a **risk-based decision** to keep the non-solid barrier, for example a risk assessment record and management approval.
practice: List all openings in the outer skin of security areas: doors, windows, loading doors, emergency exits, vents and roof skylights, and mark whether they are easily accessible.
Use security doors and break-in resistant locks, add security grilles or safety glass to windows, and keep product specifications or proof of RC2-equivalent resistance.
For sheet-metal or light partition buildings: set up a dedicated prototype security room inside, or add vibration or break-in sensors, and write a risk assessment.
Use emergency exit doors that can only be opened from inside, with door contact alarms.
Include the integrity of the outer skin in patrol checks, and immediately repair loose screws or damaged doors and windows.

questions: What kind of construction is the outer skin of the security area?
How are ground-floor windows and loading doors protected against being opened with simple tools?
Do you have proof of the break-in resistance class of doors and windows?
For the sheet-metal walls, which risk-mitigating measures did you take? Is there a risk assessment?
How are emergency exits protected against being opened from outside?
evidence: Description of the outer skin construction of security areas and list of openings.
Specifications of doors, windows and locks, or proof of break-in resistance class.
Risk assessment and approval records for non-solid construction.
Outer skin patrol and repair records.
findings: Ground-floor windows are standard aluminum windows without grilles or reinforcement.
The sheet-metal building has no reinforcement and no risk assessment.
The loading door is secured with an ordinary padlock that can easily be cut.

controls.tip: Once on site I asked: "If you were a thief, where would you get in?" The plant manager thought for three seconds and pointed at the skylight at the back. That is where your next budget should go.

controls.title: View and sight protection
controls.q_en: To what extent is view and sight protection ensured in defined security areas?
controls.q_zh: To what extent is view and sight protection ensured in defined security areas?
controls.objective: It must be ensured that unauthorized viewing of vehicles, components or parts classified as requiring protection is prevented.

must: Unauthorized viewing of new developments needing high or very high protection is not possible.
should: Sight protection through relevant glass surfaces is ensured.
View into defined security areas through open doors/gates/windows is prevented.

controls.refs: No reference standards are listed in the original (in practice, use it together with the ENX TISAX Participant Handbook and the client's prototype protection specifications)
controls.change2027: ISA 2027 renumbered section 8.1 Physical and environmental security of ISA 6 as 8.2 (former 8.1.7 visitor management moved to 8.1.8). This control corresponds to the former 8.1.4.
explain: The Must in 8.2.4 is a single sentence: unauthorized viewing of new developments needing high or very high protection is not possible. It looks simple, but the ISA's explanation is very specific: prototype parts must be protected from being seen by anyone **at any time**; workstations must be designed so they cannot be seen from outside, using covers, partition walls or fabric; and privacy screens must be designed so they cannot easily be manipulated from outside.

The ISA gives an example: external blinds on the ground floor are not sufficient, because people outside can push them aside, but they are acceptable on higher floors. For complete vehicles or vehicle superstructures, visibility must be **permanently** prevented. In addition, content shown on monitors and projectors must not be visible from outside. This is often overlooked, for example when CAD drawings are projected in a meeting room and can be clearly seen through the glass from the corridor.

The Should has two points: glass surfaces need sight protection, such as frosted film, and nobody should be able to see in through open doors, gates or windows. The most common case is a roller door opened for unloading, so the truck driver outside sees the prototypes at a glance. An inside curtain or screen can fix this.

View protection can also be combined with covering the prototypes themselves, for example black cloth or opaque packaging, and with the camouflage requirements of 8.1.2. The camouflage wrap of a test vehicle on the road is really view protection taken outside the plant.
practice: Check all glass surfaces, doors, windows and roller doors of security areas, and evaluate whether prototypes can be seen from outside or from unauthorized areas.
Apply frosted or one-way opaque film to ground-floor glass, and install screens on the inside so they cannot be operated from outside.
Add an inside curtain or a buffer zone at loading docks so that prototypes are out of direct view when the door is open.
Surround prototype workstations with partitions or curtains, and cover waiting parts with black cloth or store them in opaque containers.
Position monitors and projectors in meeting rooms and engineering offices away from windows, and apply frosted film to glass walls.
Store complete vehicles in a windowless or fully covered room.

questions: Can prototypes be seen from the corridor or parking lot outside?
When the roller door is open for unloading, what can people outside see?
How are ground-floor windows covered? Can the covers be opened from outside?
When prototype drawings are projected in the meeting room, can they be seen from outside?
Where are complete vehicles stored? How are they permanently protected from view?
evidence: View protection check records or photos (taken from outside looking in; approval required under 8.1.10).
Installation records for glass film and screening curtains.
Layout drawing of workstation partitions.
Description of view protection in the security concept.
findings: Ground-floor windows use external blinds that outsiders can simply push aside to look in.
When the loading dock is open, prototypes are directly exposed to view from outside.
The glass wall of the meeting room has no covering, and projected prototype designs can be seen from the corridor.

controls.tip: The auditor will definitely walk around the outside of the building and look in. Do the walk yourself before the assessment, once by day and once at night. At night, with the lights on, everything is especially easy to see.

controls.title: Access control (protection against unauthorized entry)
controls.q_en: To what extent is the protection against unauthorized entry regulated in the form of access control?
controls.q_zh: To what extent is the protection against unauthorized entry regulated in the form of access control?
controls.objective: It must be ensured that all points of access to security areas where vehicles, components or parts classified as requiring protection are manufactured, processed, or stored are protected against unauthorized entry by appropriate and effective measures.

must: At least one of the following three requirements must be met: Mechanical security locking units with documented key assignment, or electronic access systems with documented authorization assignment, or personal access control including documentation with access and exit times.

controls.refs: DIN 18251 (locks) or DIN EN 12209
controls.change2027: ISA 2027 renumbered section 8.1 Physical and environmental security of ISA 6 as 8.2 (former 8.1.7 visitor management moved to 8.1.8). This control corresponds to the former 8.1.5.
explain: 8.2.5 offers three options: **mechanical security locks with documented key assignment**, **electronic access control with documented authorization assignment**, or **personal access control with recorded entry and exit times**. Any of them is acceptable. The key word is "documented": who received which key, who is authorized on which card, who came in and went out when, must all be recorded.

The ISA explains that a security locking unit offers higher resistance against breaking, drilling, lockpicking or manipulation, and that keys may only be copied by authorized persons, meaning a patented or registered key system with a security card. Ordinary keys that the key shop around the corner can copy do not qualify. The reference standards are DIN 18251 and DIN EN 12209.

If you choose personal access control, for example guards recording entries and exits, you must record both entry and exit times. The ISA reminds us that these records need a maximum retention period that takes country-specific data protection law into account. The same applies to electronic access logs.

This control requires that "all points of access" are protected, including emergency exits, loading doors and internal doors to other areas. A common finding is that only the main door is controlled while a side door is left unlocked. Together with the access rights process of 8.1.7, this makes complete access management.
practice: List all points of access to the security area and confirm the control method at each one; at least one of the three options must apply.
Electronic access control: use card readers or biometrics, grant rights through the 8.1.7 process, keep the system logs and define a retention period.
Mechanical locks: use a patented key system and keep a key issue register (key number, holder, issue and return dates).
Personal access control: guards record name, entry time and exit time, and check against the authorization list.
Define a retention period for access records according to the company's data protection policy, for example 6 to 12 months, and delete them when it ends.
Install door closers and door-open alarms so that doors cannot be propped open and defeat access control.

questions: How many access points does the prototype security area have? How is each one controlled?
Can the keys be copied? Is there a record of who received which key?
Please show the electronic access authorization list and entry and exit logs.
How long are access records kept? On what basis?
What happens when a door is propped open or not closed properly?
evidence: List of access points and description of control methods.
Key issue register or access authorization list.
Entry and exit records and the rules for their retention period.
Lock specifications or proof of the patented key system.
findings: The loading door only has an ordinary lock; keys can be copied freely and there is no issue record.
Shared cards exist in the access control system, so individual entries cannot be traced.
Doors to the security area are often propped open with objects, which makes access control useless.
Access records have no retention period and are kept forever.

controls.tip: A door propped open with a cardboard box is the scene I see most often on site. A door-open alarm is cheap, but it makes access control really work.

controls.title: Intrusion monitoring
controls.q_en: To what extent are the premises to be secured monitored for intrusion?
controls.q_zh: To what extent are the premises to be secured monitored for intrusion?
controls.objective: It must be ensured that premises where vehicles, components or parts classified as requiring protection are manufactured, processed, or stored are monitored for intrusion.

must: An intrusion detection system exists with alarm tracking to a qualified security service or control center (e.g. according to DIN 77200, VdS 3138), or 24/7 guarding by a qualified security service.
Alarm plans are available.
Timely alarm processing is ensured.

controls.change2027: ISA 2027 renumbered section 8.1 Physical and environmental security of ISA 6 as 8.2 (former 8.1.7 visitor management moved to 8.1.8). This control corresponds to the former 8.1.6.
explain: 8.2.6 requires intrusion monitoring, with two possible approaches: an **intrusion detection system** whose alarms are sent to a **qualified security service or control center**, or **24/7 guarding** by a qualified security service. The ISA refers to DIN 77200 and VdS 3138, the German standards for security services and alarm receiving centers. Outside Germany, in practice you choose a licensed security company and define the monitoring and response requirements in the contract.

Video recording alone is not intrusion monitoring. CCTV is reviewed after the fact, while intrusion detection discovers and reports in real time. If the alarm only sounds inside the plant and nobody hears it after working hours, it is not effective either. It must be connected to a staffed control center.

The second and third Must are alarm plans and timely alarm handling. The ISA explains that, as a rule, an alarm intervention must take place within a maximum of **twenty minutes**. So the security contract must state the response time, and you must keep alarm and response records as proof.

The alarm plan must clearly describe: which zone was triggered, who must be informed, how the security service verifies the alarm, who goes on site, whether the police are called, and how the prototype protection officer and the client are informed afterwards. It must be linked to 8.1.11 incident management.
practice: Install door contacts, infrared motion detectors, glass-break sensors and similar sensors at entrances, windows and the roof of security areas, and arm the system after working hours.
Sign a remote monitoring contract with a licensed security company that defines alarm receipt, response time (for example on site within twenty minutes) and the notification process.
Alternatively, have 24-hour on-site security guards, and keep the shift schedules and patrol records.
Write an alarm plan: zone list, notification list, handling steps, and the link to the 8.1.11 incident procedure and client notification.
Get monthly alarm and response reports from the security company, and review false alarms and response times.
Test sensors and connections regularly, and keep test records.

questions: How are prototype areas monitored for intrusion after working hours?
Where are alarms sent? Is the security company qualified?
Please show the alarm plan.
How soon does the security service arrive after an alarm? Are there records?
What caused the most recent alarm? How was it handled?
How often are the sensors tested?
evidence: Layout of the intrusion detection system and zone list.
Remote monitoring contract or on-site guarding contract.
Alarm plan.
Alarm and response records, test records.
findings: There is only CCTV recording, with no intrusion detection or real-time reporting.
The alarm only sounds inside the plant and is not connected to a security control center.
There is no alarm plan, and the security service does not know whom to inform.
The response time to alarms cannot be proven.

controls.tip: Write the twenty minutes into the security contract. When the auditor asks about response time, showing the contract and the response reports is a hundred times stronger than a verbal promise.

controls.title: On-site client segregation
controls.q_en: To what extent is on-site client segregation existent?
controls.q_zh: To what extent is on-site client segregation existent?
controls.objective: In order to ensure protection of the client-specific know-how at all times, a clear segregation of clients must be ensured. This particularly involves protection against unauthorized viewing and access to areas where vehicles, components or parts classified as requiring protection are processed or stored.

must: There is a spatial separation through personnel, organizational or technical measures. The following aspects are considered: – Customers and/or; – Projects; – Where segregation is not in effect, explicit approval by the customer is required.

controls.refs: No reference standards are listed in the original (in practice, use it together with the ENX TISAX Participant Handbook and the client's prototype protection specifications)
controls.change2027: ISA 2027 renumbered section 8.1 Physical and environmental security of ISA 6 as 8.2 (former 8.1.7 visitor management moved to 8.1.8). This control corresponds to the former 8.1.8.
explain: Many Tier 1 and Tier 2 suppliers serve several OEMs at the same time. 8.2.7 requires **client segregation**: when people from OEM A visit, they must not see the prototypes of OEM B. Segregation can be by customer or by project, and it can use personnel, organizational or technical measures.

Spatial separation can be done at several levels: separate rooms, areas enclosed by partitions or curtains, time slots for different customers on the same equipment, and different staff for different customers. The key is preventing unauthorized **viewing** and **access**.

If segregation really is not possible, for example when a large test rig is shared, the ISA allows an exception, but the customer's **explicit approval** is required, preferably in writing. This should also be agreed as part of the 8.1.2 order-specific requirements.
Pay special attention to the visitor route during customer audits or tours. Where needed, temporarily cover other customers' prototypes, and escort visitors at all times according to 8.1.8.
practice: Mark the dedicated areas for each customer or project on the floor plan, and separate them with access control or partitions.
Group access rights by customer / project so that people can only enter the areas they are responsible for.
Use shared equipment in time slots; when switching customers, clear the area and cover other customers' items.
Plan the route before customer visits and cover other customers' prototypes along the way.
Where segregation is not possible, get the customer's written consent and file it.
Use codes on prototype labels instead of showing the customer name and vehicle model directly.

questions: How many customers' prototypes are on site at the same time? How are they segregated?
When customer A visits, how do you ensure they cannot see customer B's prototypes?
How is shared equipment handled?
Are there cases without segregation? Where is the customer's approval?
Are people's access rights separated by customer or project?
evidence: Floor plan showing client segregation.
Access rights settings grouped by customer.
Schedules for shared equipment and records of clearing the area.
Customer's written approval for cases without segregation.
findings: Prototypes of several customers are mixed on the same rack without any covering.
The route for customer visits passes through another customer's prototype area.
Shared test equipment is used without the customers' consent.

controls.tip: The most awkward scene I have seen: an auditor from OEM A pointed at a new part for OEM B on the line and asked, "Whose is this?" The whole floor went silent. Planning the visitor route really matters.

summary: 8.2.1: establish a security concept covering six aspects (outer skin, view protection, access control, intrusion monitoring, visitor management, client segregation), plus perimeter security as a Should.
8.2.2 Perimeter: unauthorized access to the property must not be possible; structural, technical and natural barriers can be combined.

8.2.3 Outer skin: easily accessible doors and windows must resist simple tools such as screwdrivers and pliers for at least three minutes; a non-solid structure needs risk-mitigating measures and evidence of a risk-based decision.

8.2.4 View protection: new developments classified high or very high must not be viewable by unauthorized persons; watch out for external blinds on the ground floor, loading docks, monitors and projectors.
8.2.5 Access control: one of three options (mechanical security locks, electronic access control or personal access control), documented; set a retention period for entry and exit records.

8.2.6 Intrusion monitoring: intrusion detection connected to a qualified security service or control center, or 24/7 qualified guards; alarm plans and timely handling, with intervention as a rule within twenty minutes.
8.2.7 Client segregation: spatial separation by customer and/or project; without segregation, the customer's explicit approval is required.

lines.text: Wow, we have finally reached the prototype protection module! In this part, we first learn what a prototype requiring protection is, and then look at 8.1.1 and 8.1.2.

slide.title: Introduction to prototype protection
bullets: What is a prototype requiring protection

lines.text: Hello everyone, I am Allan. Speaking of prototypes, let me ask you first. Have you ever seen one of those strange cars on the highway, covered in black and white patterns?
Yes, yes! Those cars that look like zebras! I thought they were some kind of art cars!
That is a camouflage wrap. Car makers use it so you cannot see the lines of the new model clearly. It is the most famous image of prototype protection.
The ISA says prototypes include vehicles, components and parts, and the owner of the intellectual property for a prototype is considered the owner of the prototype.

slide.title: Who decides?
bullets: Owner = owner of the intellectual property
High or very high: minimum requirements apply

lines.text: So does the supplier decide whether a part needs protection?
No. The owner's commissioning department does the classification. If a prototype is classified as high or very high, the minimum requirements of this module must be applied.

I once met a supplier who said, it is only a plastic bracket, surely it does not need protection? But the customer's drawing clearly had a classification stamp on it. That is simply not your decision.
So which TISAX prototype labels are there?
There are four common ones: Proto parts, Proto vehicles, Test vehicles and Proto events. They usually need an AL3 on-site assessment.
But please note, ISA 2027 deleted the former sections 8.3 to 8.5. Test vehicles, events and shoots are now covered by the order-specific requirements in 8.1.2.
So for the controls each label is assessed against under ISA 2027, always check the latest ENX Participant Handbook. Do not rely on memory.
Let me take notes! 8.1 is now organizational requirements, 8.2 is physical security, and 8.3 to 8.5 are deleted!

slide.title: ISA 2027 restructuring
bullets: Six new controls, such as 8.1.1 and 8.1.2

lines.text: Very good. Now let us go to the first control, 8.1.1, prototype protection regulations and responsibilities.
It requires a released prototype protection policy that clearly states goals and specifications. It must be reviewed regularly and revised when needed.
What does released mean? We have a copy of the customer's specification. Is that okay?
The customer's specification is a good reference, but the policy must be approved and published by your own company. Auditors will not accept a draft or a copy.
For responsibilities, they must be defined, documented and assigned. The responsible people must be qualified, resources must be in place, and contact persons must be known inside and outside.
What I see most often is that prototype protection is a side job for general affairs. I ask how many customer projects are on site, and the answer is, I need to ask sales first.
Ha ha, the auditor would frown right away!
Right. So even though 2027.1 removed the Should from 8.1.1, you must do the remaining Must requirements one by one even more carefully.
Next is the highlight of ISA 2027, 8.1.2, order-specific requirements!
This control requires that for every relevant order, you agree specific requirements with the customer and make them known to the people doing the work. The ISA lists nine aspects.
Classification, camouflage and changes to camouflage, test sites, public roads, events, shoots, transport and logistics, subcontractors, and portable storage media.
But we only make interior parts and never drive on the road. Do we have to write all nine?
Good question. You can mark them not applicable, but write a reason. That proves you thought about each one and did not simply forget it.

I once worked with a lamp maker. Sales kept the customer's confidentiality annex in a mailbox, and the driver shipped the prototypes in a truck with a canvas cover. Everyone on the highway could see them.
Wow, so the order requirements never reached the shop floor?
Exactly. So I recommend a one-page order checklist. Tick the nine aspects, then turn them into work instructions that shop-floor people can understand.
Camouflage needs attention too. If the wrap is torn, you cannot just patch it with tape. You must follow the customer's rules for changes to camouflage.

slide.title: What the auditor asks
bullets: Pick an order and explain its requirements
May prototype data go on a USB drive?

lines.text: The auditor usually picks an order, asks you what you agreed with the customer, and then goes on site to ask the workers if they know, right?
Exactly right. ARALE, you could already work as an auditor.

Summary: the client decides the classification, 8.1.1 needs a released policy and clear responsibilities, and 8.1.2 means agreeing each aspect per order and passing it to the shop floor. Next, training, people and NDAs!
In this part, we look at four controls about people: 8.1.3 training, 8.1.4 qualification, 8.1.5 non-disclosure agreements and 8.1.6 subcontractors.
In prototype protection, the weakest link is usually people. Let us start with 8.1.3, training.

slide.title: 8.1.3 Training and awareness
bullets: Training at least once a year
Part of the overall training concept, 2.1.3

lines.text: The ISA requires training at least once a year, plus training at the start of each project. Participation is mandatory for all project members, and records must be kept.
What is the difference between annual training and project-start training?
Annual training covers general rules, like the photography ban and escorting visitors. Project-start training covers this customer's specific requirements, the things agreed under 8.1.2.
The control question uses the word evidently. That means you must be able to prove it. The auditor will compare the access control list with the training list.
I saw one company with eighty people on the access list but only fifty on the training attendance list. Most of the missing thirty were agency workers and resident engineers.
Oh no, agency workers and resident engineers are so often forgotten.
Also, prototype training must be part of the company's overall training concept, which links to Information Security 2.1.3. Do not create a separate system that nobody manages.
Next is a new control in ISA 2027, 8.1.4, qualification of staff in prototype areas!

slide.title: 8.1.4 Qualification of staff
bullets: Must: define and meet job requirements

lines.text: First, identify which jobs are sensitive, such as pre-series assembly, prototype warehouse staff and test drivers. Then define requirements for these jobs and make sure they are met.
You must also verify the identity of potential employees, for example by checking their ID card. The Should is to check suitability with simple methods, like a job interview.
So do we need police clearance certificates or background checks?
The ISA deliberately says simple methods. It does not require background checks. Also respect your national data protection and employment laws, and do not collect too much data.
My advice: for the identity check, just keep a tick box and the checker's signature. You do not have to keep a copy of the ID card, which also lowers the data protection risk.
Next is 8.1.5, non-disclosure agreements!

slide.title: 8.1.5 Non-disclosure agreements
bullets: Company level: NDA with the customer
Individual level: employees and project members
Can be part of the employment contract

lines.text: NDAs have two levels: company to customer, and company to all employees and project members. You need both, and they must be valid under local contract law.
The good news: the ISA says the employees' confidentiality obligation can be in the employment contract. Only people not covered by the contract need to sign separately.
Like agency workers, interns and consultants. They are not in an employment contract, so they sign separately, right?
Right. And the biggest risk with NDAs is expiry. I once saw a customer NDA that had expired three years earlier, but prototypes were still arriving every month.
Wow, so there was a hole in the legal protection!
So I suggest putting NDAs in a contract management system with expiry reminders, and adding an NDA in force checkpoint to the project opening process.
Finally, 8.1.6, commissioning subcontractors.

slide.title: 8.1.6 Subcontractors
bullets: Meet customer security needs, get proof

lines.text: Three things: approval by the original customer, a valid NDA with the subcontractor, and making sure the subcontractor meets the actual customer's security requirements, with proof.
Here is a true story. A company sent a prototype housing to an external paint shop. The owner of the paint shop loved the color, took a photo and posted it on Facebook.
No way! So the look of the new car leaked completely!
Yes, and the car maker called the next day. So before subcontracting, get customer approval and proof from the subcontractor, for example a TISAX label or your own audit.
One more point: the approval must go back to the original customer. Your customer may be a Tier 1, but the real owner of the prototype is the car maker.
The auditor will ask: which prototype work is subcontracted now? Where is the customer approval? When does the subcontractor's TISAX label expire?

slide.title: Common findings
bullets: Prototypes received under an expired NDA

lines.text: Very good. What these four controls have in common is people and contracts. Records must be complete, and the lists must match.
Summary: training every year plus at project start, identify sensitive jobs, NDAs at both levels, and subcontracting needs approval plus proof. Next, access process, visitors, phones and photos!

video.title: 8.1.7–8.1.10 Access Rights, Visitors, Phones and Photography

lines.text: This part is the one everyone can relate to: access rights, visitor management, carrying phones, and rules for taking photos!
For these four controls, the auditor starts watching the moment they walk through the main gate. Let us start with 8.1.7.

slide.title: 8.1.7 Access rights process
bullets: Code of conduct for loss or theft
Disable cards or change locks quickly

lines.text: This control is about the process: who approves, how rights are added, changed and revoked, and when a card or key is lost or stolen, what employees do and how the company disables it quickly.
But 8.2.5 is also about access control. What is the difference?
8.1.7 is the process, 8.2.5 is the technical means. One controls who may enter, the other controls how the door is locked.
The auditor's favorite trick is to compare the latest leavers list with the access control system. In five minutes, they see whether the process really works.
Once I picked an engineer who had left three months earlier, and his card still worked. HR said, we informed them. Facilities said, we never got anything.
Ha ha, the classic game of passing the ball between departments!
Next is 8.1.8, visitor management. It changed in 2027.1!
Visitor management moved from 8.1.7 in ISA 6 to 8.1.8, and 2027.1 added including traceable documentation to the objective.
So you must be able to trace who came, when, whom they visited, which areas they entered and when they left. All visitors register, sign confidentiality before entry, and the rules are published.
And escorting. The title is very clear. Visitors in prototype areas must be escorted by an employee all the time. They cannot walk around on their own.
What about the boss's good friend, or the customer's big boss? Do they need to register too?
That is the sentence I hear most in consulting: he is a friend of the boss. And of course, that is the day the auditor is standing at the main gate.
A rule is only a rule if it is the same for everyone. Also, a paper visitor book should not let the next visitor see everyone's phone numbers. That is a data protection issue.
Next is the one I am most curious about, 8.1.9. Can I take my phone in or not?

slide.title: 8.1.9 Mobile recording devices
bullets: Carrying rules: camera sealed or not
Usage rules: calls, photos, QR codes
Only works with checks at entry and exit

lines.text: The ISA requires two kinds of rules. Rules for carrying, for example whether the camera is sealed. And rules for use, for example whether you may make calls, take photos or scan QR codes.
In many plants, the most common method is camera stickers. At entry, the guard puts tamper-evident stickers on the front and rear cameras. At exit, the guard checks them.
I know those stickers! When you peel them off, the word VOID appears, right?
Right. But the danger is that it becomes a formality and nobody checks. At exit, the guard must really turn the phone over. If a sticker is broken, record it and report it.
I also saw someone with perfectly sealed phone cameras walk in wearing a smartwatch with a camera. So the rules should cover any device that can record.
And finally, what about the photography rules in 8.1.10?

slide.title: 8.1.10 Image recording
bullets: Record who, when, what, where, which device

lines.text: The principle is a general ban on photos. An exception needs release by the original client, an internal approval process, and a record of who, when, what, where and with which device.
The client decides how the images are classified. After the shoot, store them securely, send them only to authorized people, and delete them securely when no longer needed.
Quality staff often need to photograph defective parts for the customer. That is very common, right?
Extremely common. And the finding I see most in assessments is quality staff using their own phones and posting the photos in a chat group like WhatsApp or LINE.
Oh no, then the photos end up on everyone's phone.
The fix is simple: one numbered camera, one request form, photos in an encrypted project folder, and sending them through the platform the customer specifies.

Summary: 8.1.7 is the process for who may enter, 8.1.8 means every visitor registers and is traceable, 8.1.9 needs carrying and usage rules, and 8.1.10 bans photos in principle. Next, incidents and disposal!
The last three organizational controls are all new in ISA 2027! Incident management, traceability, and disposal and recycling.
These three complete the life cycle of a prototype: what to do when something goes wrong, where it is now, and where it goes at the end.

slide.title: 8.1.11 Incident management
bullets: Procedures agreed per order with client

lines.text: 8.1.11 requires that for every order, incident procedures are agreed with the client, nine situations are considered, and the relevant employees know them.
How is that different from incident management in Information Security 1.6?
1.6 is the company-wide mechanism. 8.1.11 is per order and agreed with the client. You can put them in the same procedure, but write the client's reporting path separately.
The nine situations are: breach of secrecy, burglary, theft, breakdowns, accidents, fire, irregularities in transport, dealing with authorities and law enforcement, and damage to camouflage.
Dealing with authorities and law enforcement? What kind of situation is that?

For example, a test vehicle has an accident and the police want to take photos as evidence, or customs want to open a box with a prototype. The driver must know what to say and must inform the client contact at once.
Or the camouflage wrap gets torn by the wind on the highway and flaps like a flag. Do you pull over or keep driving? The response card must say clearly.
Ha ha, a car flying a flag down the highway must be quite a sight!
Also, incident handling may still matter after the order ends, for example if photos leak after the project. And reporting duties and channels must be known internally and by the client.
I recommend one tabletop exercise a year. Take one scenario and let everyone say the next step. Usually by step three you find something nobody thought of.
Next is 8.1.12, documentation and traceability.
The objective is very direct: at any time, you must be able to trace where a prototype is and which department is currently responsible for it.
You need a process or concept, every prototype must be recorded, changes must be traceable, and the documentation must be updated regularly.
Auditors love the two-way check. They pick an entry from the register and find the item on site, then pick an item on site and look for its record.
Wow, it would be bad if there is a part on site that is not in the register.
That really happened to me. There was a box of parts on site, and everyone said, not mine. In the end, it turned out to be prototypes left over from the previous project.
I suggest code labels or QR codes, so one scan updates the location. Do not write the vehicle model on the label. That alone would be a leak.
The last one is 8.1.13, disposal, recycling and return!

slide.title: 8.1.13 Disposal, recycling, return
bullets: Includes relevant tools, e.g. press dies

lines.text: The ISA stresses that prototypes must not be thrown away as standard waste. The Must is to get the client's rules for disposal, recycling or return, and to inform the affected employees.
The Should is proof of compliance, for example return receipts, destruction certificates, or destruction records witnessed by two people.
I saw that the ISA also mentions relevant tools. What does that mean?
These are tools made specifically for producing prototype parts, such as body press dies. The die itself contains design information, so at project end it must also follow the customer's rules.
In assessments, I always walk to the recycling yard behind the plant. Once I found a bumper that was not yet on the market in the scrap pile. The plant manager turned pale.
However good the access control is, if it ends up in the scrap yard, all that work is wasted.

slide.title: Common findings
bullets: Only a generic security incident procedure
Register and items do not match

lines.text: Exactly. Put these three controls together and you have the full story of a prototype, from entering the plant to leaving it.

Summary: incidents are agreed per order for nine situations, you always know where a prototype is and who owns it, and disposal follows client rules, dies included. Next chapter: 8.2 physical security!

video.title: 8.2.1–8.2.3 Security Concept, Perimeter and Outer Skin

lines.text: Welcome to part two of prototype protection, physical and environmental security! In this part we look at 8.2.1 to 8.2.3.
8.2 applies to companies that manufacture or store prototypes on their own property, or that are given prototypes to use. I like to think of it as an onion.
An onion? Allan, are you starting with the comparisons again?
The outer layer is the perimeter, then the building's outer skin, then cannot be seen, cannot get in, and someone knows. The innermost layer is segregation between customers.
And 8.2.1, the security concept, draws the whole onion as one picture.

The security concept must consider six aspects: stable outer skin, view protection, protection against unauthorized entry and access control, intrusion monitoring, documented visitor management, and client segregation.
The Should adds perimeter security. The ISA also says the operator of the property is responsible for establishing and implementing it.
So does the security concept need to be a thick document?
No. What I recommend most is one clearly marked floor plan plus one table for the six aspects. The auditor walks around with the plan, and if it matches, that is a big plus.
The worst case is a floor plan from three years ago. The site has been extended, the prototype area moved to the next building, but on the plan it is still in the old place.
Next is 8.2.2, perimeter security!

slide.title: 8.2.2 Perimeter security
bullets: Must: sum of measures is enough

lines.text: The Must focuses on the result: unauthorized access to the property must not be possible, and the sum of measures must be enough. You can combine walls, fences, detection, alarms and even plants.
The ISA also mentions floor count. If the prototype area is on a high floor, that alone makes access harder. Companies in shared buildings can make good use of this.
What about a plant in an industrial park that shares a wall with the factory next door?
Then explain it in the security concept and make the inner layers stronger. A hole in the perimeter is acceptable, as long as you know where it is and the next layer is strong enough.
I once saw a side gate held open with a brick all day so goods could move faster. The guard said, the boss said this way is quicker.
The boss again! The boss really shows up a lot!
Next is the famous 8.2.3, the three-minute rule!

slide.title: 8.2.3 Outer skin against break-in
bullets: Accessible doors and windows resist tools

lines.text: Easily accessible windows, doors and other components must resist break-in with simple tools like screwdrivers and pliers for at least three minutes. The reference standard is DIN EN 1627, RC2.
Can we easily buy doors and windows labeled RC2 outside Europe?
Not always. In practice, you can use equivalent security doors, reinforced locks and security grilles, and keep the specifications or a confirmation from the manufacturer.
Easily accessible is the key word. Ground-floor windows, loading doors, emergency exits and roof skylights are the common weak spots.
Sheet-metal buildings are the hardest. With a power screwdriver, you can remove a wall panel in a few minutes. This is where the Should comes in.
The Should prefers solid construction like masonry or concrete. If it is not solid, you need risk-mitigating measures and evidence of a risk-based decision.
So in a sheet-metal building, you can build a dedicated prototype room inside, add vibration detection, and write a risk assessment!
ARALE, you get it. On site I often ask the plant manager: if you were a thief, where would you get in? After three seconds he points at the skylight. That is the next budget item.

slide.title: Common findings
bullets: Floor plan does not match the site
Plain aluminum windows on ground floor

lines.text: Summary: 8.2.1 is a concept with six aspects plus perimeter, 8.2.2 means the sum of measures prevents access, and 8.2.3 means weak points resist simple tools for three minutes. Next, view protection and access control!
In this part, prototypes become invisible and unreachable! 8.2.4 view protection and 8.2.5 access control.

slide.title: Cannot be seen, cannot get in

lines.text: The biggest fear with prototypes is not only theft, but being seen. One photo can reveal a new car design too early.

slide.title: 8.2.4 View protection
bullets: Must: high or very high not viewable
Should: no view through open doors

lines.text: The Must is a single sentence: new developments needing high or very high protection must not be viewable by unauthorized persons.
The ISA's explanation is very specific: it must be possible to hide prototype parts from anyone at any time, and workstations must not be visible from outside, using covers, partitions or fabric.
So if we put blinds on the windows, that should be fine, right?
The ISA uses exactly that example. External blinds on the ground floor are not enough, because people outside can push them aside. On higher floors, they are acceptable.
Complete vehicles or vehicle superstructures must be permanently hidden. And the content of monitors and projectors must not be visible from outside either.
In one company, I stood in the corridor and saw a 3D lamp design on the projector screen through the meeting room glass. The people inside were still having a serious meeting.
Wow, that is a live broadcast of a new car design!
The Should has two points: glass needs sight protection, like frosted film, and nobody should see in through open doors, gates or windows.
The most common case is the loading dock. When the roller door goes up, the truck driver outside sees a whole row of prototypes. One curtain on the inside solves it.
I know! It is the same idea as the camouflage wrap on a test vehicle. It takes view protection outside the plant!
Well said. I also suggest walking around the outside of the building before the assessment, once by day and once at night. At night, with the lights on, everything is easy to see.
Next is 8.2.5, access control!

slide.title: 8.2.5 Access control: one of three
bullets: Mechanical locks plus key issue records
Personal control plus entry and exit times

lines.text: Every access point needs at least one of three options: security locks with documented key assignment, electronic access with documented authorization, or personal control with recorded entry and exit times.
How is a security lock different from a normal lock?
The ISA says a security lock gives higher resistance against breaking, drilling, lockpicking and manipulation, and keys can only be copied by authorized persons.
So the kind of key the shop around the corner can copy in three minutes does not count. You need a patented key system or one with a security card.
If you choose personal control, you must record entry and exit times. The ISA also reminds us that these records need a maximum retention period that respects data protection law.
So the access logs cannot be kept forever?
Right. Set a retention period, for example six months to one year according to the company's data protection policy, and delete them after that. This fits the spirit of data protection.
And another very common scene: the access control system is great, but the door is propped open with a cardboard box, because moving goods is a hassle.
Oh no, then even the best access control is useless.
Install a door-open alarm and a door closer. It does not cost much, but it makes access control really work. And do not forget to combine it with the access rights process in 8.1.7.

slide.title: Common findings
bullets: Ground-floor blinds can be pushed aside
Prototypes exposed at the loading dock

lines.text: Summary: under 8.2.4, high or very high new developments must not be seen, so watch blinds, loading docks and screens. Under 8.2.5, pick one of three access options and document it. Next, intrusion and segregation!
The last part of prototype protection! 8.2.6 intrusion monitoring and 8.2.7 client segregation. After this, we have finished the whole module.
So far we covered cannot be seen and cannot get in. 8.2.6 is about this: if someone forces their way in, someone must know.

slide.title: 8.2.6 Intrusion monitoring
bullets: Detection linked to qualified security service
Or 24/7 guarding by a qualified service
Timely response, as a rule within 20 min

lines.text: There are two approaches: an intrusion detection system connected to a qualified security service or control center, or round-the-clock guards from a qualified security service, 24 hours a day, every day.

The ISA refers to DIN 77200 and VdS 3138, which are German standards for security services. Elsewhere, companies usually choose a licensed security company and write the requirements into the contract.
Our factory has lots of cameras. Does that count?
Camera recordings are reviewed afterwards. Intrusion monitoring detects and reports in real time. They are different. CCTV alone is usually not enough.
I saw a plant where the alarm only sounded inside the building. After hours, the whole industrial park was empty. The alarm rang all night, and the cleaning lady found it the next morning.
Wow, so who was that alarm ringing for?
There are two more Must requirements: alarm plans, and timely handling of alarms. The ISA explains that, as a rule, intervention must happen within twenty minutes.
So write the twenty minutes into the security contract, and review the alarm and response reports from the security company every month. When the auditor asks, showing them is very convincing.
So what should the alarm plan include?

Which zone was triggered, whom to inform, how the security service verifies it, who goes on site, whether to call the police, and how to inform the prototype protection officer and the client afterwards.
This must connect to 8.1.11 incident management. Burglary and theft are already two of the nine situations there.
The last control, 8.2.7, client segregation!

slide.title: 8.2.7 Client segregation
bullets: Separate by customer, project or both

lines.text: Many Tier 1 and Tier 2 suppliers serve several car makers at once. 8.2.7 requires spatial separation by customer or project, using personnel, organizational or technical measures.
If segregation is really impossible, for example a large shared test rig, you must get the customer's explicit approval, preferably in writing.
Does client segregation always mean building a separate room?
Not necessarily. Partitions, curtains, time slots, access rights grouped by customer, and different staff for different customers are all workable options.
The most awkward scene I have seen: an auditor from car maker A pointed at a new part for car maker B on the line and asked, whose is this? The whole floor went silent.
Oh my, the atmosphere must have been really tense.
So always plan the route before customer visits, cover other customers' prototypes along the way, and escort visitors at all times according to 8.1.8.
And use codes on labels. Do not write the customer name and vehicle model directly. Even the signs on the racks can leak information.

slide.title: Common findings
bullets: Alarm not linked to a security center

lines.text: Finally, let me sum up the whole prototype protection module for everyone!

slide.title: Prototype module summary
bullets: Check label mapping in ENX handbook

lines.text: 8.1 organizational requirements cover policy, orders, people, contracts, processes and the life cycle. 8.2 physical security is each layer of the onion. You need both together.
One last reminder: for how prototype labels map to controls under ISA 2027, always check the latest ENX Participant Handbook.

Summary: intrusion alarms go to a qualified security service, or guards are there around the clock, with intervention within twenty minutes. No segregation means customer approval. Module done. Great work, everyone!
